findings.title: record_stored_segments now invoked per flusher buffer instead of once on writer
findings.body: The pre-change code called `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` once per `submit()` on the writer buffer. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()`, which is once per flusher process. With multiple flusher processes this multiplies invocations by N, and crucially drops the call on the actual writer buffer (the original `buffer` argument is no longer stored on `self`). If `record_stored_segments` is a metric emission that tags state, has side effects in Redis, or otherwise isn't idempotent across processes, this is a metric/state regression. Even if it is just a gauge, the cardinality and emission frequency for downstream metrics change.

findings.title: Dead helper _create_process_for_shard is never called
findings.body: The newly introduced `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is never invoked anywhere in the module. It is a leftover that duplicates the work of `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` but is unreachable. Leaving dead public-looking methods around risks future callers assuming restart-by-shard works when the mapping actually restarts whole processes.

findings.title: Killed processes are not joined; replace-by-key can leak zombies
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the old process is killed (when it is a `multiprocessing.Process`) and then immediately replaced in `self.processes[process_index]` by a brand-new process without joining the previous one. The previous process object loses its last reference and becomes a zombie until its finalizer runs. In `join()` the loop calls `process.terminate()` on the still-stored entries but again never joins, leaving zombies for `terminate`d processes. Over many restart cycles this can pile up zombie PIDs and consume resources; combined with the spawn context it is also easy to lose visibility into why flusher processes vanished.

findings.title: Restart path leaves the previous thread (test mode) running with stale buffer
findings.body: `_ensure_processes_alive` only kills `multiprocessing.Process` instances; `threading.Thread` instances (created when `produce_to_pipe` is set, e.g. in tests) are explicitly not killed. The new process/thread is then started with a fresh `SpansBuffer`, but the old thread keeps running against its original buffer and continues to call the (now stale) `produce_to_pipe`. In a unit test this can produce phantom messages or assertions against the wrong buffer; in any future deployment that uses threading it would silently leak work. Either always join both kinds, or explicitly document that thread mode is single-shot.

findings.title: process_restarts accumulates across the lifetime of the consumer
findings.body: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is incremented on every unhealthy detection and never reset. Combined with the `>` comparison (which lets the count reach `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS + 1 == 11` before raising), any flusher process that crashes 12 times over the consumer's lifetime (including rare, isolated crashes months apart) will permanently take the consumer down with `RuntimeError`. The counter should reset after the process has been healthy for some interval, and the comparison should be `>=` if the intent is exactly `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` restarts.

findings.title: if not process: continue is dead code
findings.body: `self.processes[process_index]` is always assigned a `multiprocessing.Process` or `threading.Thread` instance in `_create_process_for_shards`; both are truthy. The `if not process: continue` guard can never fire and should be removed (or replaced with the actual invariant you want to enforce).

findings.title: Class docstring claims one process per shard but default caps processes at 1
findings.body: The class docstring now reads 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' But the constructor computes `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, and the new CLI flag `flusher_processes` defaults to 1, so the actual production default is one shared process for all shards. The docstring (and the PR description: 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard') overstates the behavior at default settings. Either reword the docstring/helper text to reflect the 'up to N processes, defaulting to 1' semantics, or change the default to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` to actually deliver 'one process per shard' out of the box.

findings.title: --flusher-processes help text and default contradict the PR description
findings.body: The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to `1` and its help string says 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' The PR description says 'let's make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard.' With the default of 1, every shard will be multiplexed onto a single process (because `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` collapses to 1). Operators who read the help text will not realize they have to set `--flusher-processes=<num_shards>` to actually get the documented one-process-per-shard layout. Either set the default to the shard count, or document the trade-off in the option help and in the SpanFlusher docstring.

findings.title: join() never calls terminate on hung threads and can deadlock the consumer
findings.body: In `join()`, the wait loop only sleeps until `process.is_alive()` is false or the deadline elapses, and only calls `process.terminate()` for `multiprocessing.Process`. A hung `threading.Thread` (which happens any time `produce_to_pipe` is set) will block `join()` until the deadline. Worse, the loop terminates by calling `process.terminate()` only on the entry currently iterated, with no `process.join()` afterwards; any process that survives past the deadline (e.g. spawn-context process that ignores SIGTERM) will be left as a zombie. Add explicit `join(timeout)` after `terminate()` for both kinds, and a fallback to `_stopped` polling for threads.

findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is monkeypatched to a no-op
findings.body: The test does `monkeypatch.setattr('time.sleep', lambda _: None)` and then immediately calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with a comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change.' Because of the monkeypatch that call is a no-op, so the comment is misleading and the test does not actually yield to let the (now threaded) flusher catch up on the new drift. The earlier `step.poll()` does not flush either. The test currently still passes because the spawn-context flusher thread races quickly, but this is a latent flake and the comment lies about behavior. Either remove the no-op sleep, drop the comment, or use `event.wait`/an actual non-patched sleep.

findings.title: test_flusher_processes_limit only checks structure, not correctness of shared-shard flushing
findings.body: The new test creates 4 partitions, sets `flusher_processes=2`, and only asserts that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`. It never submits a single message, never produces a KafkaPayload, and never verifies that shards are actually distributed (e.g. that processes share shards correctly, that the buffer the flusher uses is the right one, that segments from every shard eventually flush). The most important behavioral claim of the PR — that multiple shards sharing one flusher process still works — is not tested.

findings.title: test_backpressure relies on a sleep that is not patched and is likely flaky
findings.body: `append` uses `sleep` imported via `from time import sleep`, which is a local name bound at import time and is *not* affected by `monkeypatch.setattr('time.sleep', ...)`. So `sleep(1.0)` actually blocks for a real second on each produced payload, while the inner flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` is patched to a no-op. After the 0.1s real sleep, the flusher thread is still blocked inside the very first `append` call and `messages` is empty, so `assert messages` is racing against the producer. The test happens to pass today only because the flusher has not yet produced when the assertion runs, but the assertion is timing-dependent and the comment/help text does not warn about this. Use a sentinel (e.g. set a flag on the first call) instead of sleeping for a wall-clock second, or monkeypatch the local symbol.
